Thanks. I found Q3 quite challenging – balancing privacy and helpfulness felt really difficult. The incremental nature of adding data was good, forcing us to think specifically about each step. But ‘improvement’ wasn't always clearly defined; improvement *for whom*?

I think Q4, the explainability section, is crucial. As an advisor, I *need* to understand why a student is flagged, even if it means fewer students are identified. 

Looking at the results, there's strong agreement on rejecting sensitive data unless it improves fairness – that’s encouraging. My answers were perhaps more cautious regarding Absalon data; I worry about interpreting online behaviour without understanding context. Maybe an opt-out for data collection could resolve some concerns?

Thanks. I agree with A2 about Q3 being tough – it’s a real balancing act. As an international student working part-time, my own situation feels quite…visible already. So, ‘improvement’ really resonated; improvement *for the student*, not just statistically.

I found Q4 important too, but maybe for different reasons. I'd want to know *why* I was flagged – that’s about trust. But given my background, I might be unfairly penalised by some criteria. 

Seeing almost everyone said ‘never’ to age, gender and race felt strong. It validated my discomfort with those questions. My answers on nationality and financial aid were slightly more open if it helped, but only because of fairness – ensuring the model doesn't disadvantage students like me already facing extra challenges. An opt-out is a good idea, absolutely.

Thanks both of you. I agree with A2 that Q3 was difficult – defining “improvement” felt vague. For me, it’s not just *statistical* improvement; it's about improving outcomes for students who are already struggling, and the potential for data to be misinterpreted. As someone with dyslexia, I worry about assumptions made based on things like online activity – is slow page loading due to understanding difficulties, or something else?

Q4 was most important for me, absolutely. Explainability builds trust, especially as someone who needs extra time in exams - a black box just isn't helpful. I’m glad everyone strongly rejected those sensitive data points, although my slight willingness on disability-related info reflects needing accommodations *being* known to the university already; it feels different. That opt-out is vital.

Thanks both of you. I agree with A2 and S7 – Q3 *was* difficult. As an advisor, I see how easily data can be misinterpreted. “Improvement” needs to be carefully defined - is it simply more flags, or genuinely helping the right students? The incremental approach was good though, forcing us to weigh each addition.

For me, Q5, about fairness, is paramount. We *must* ensure this model doesn't exacerbate existing inequalities; equal recall feels essential. I worry less about a slight dip in overall identification if it means equitable support. 

I found my answers fairly aligned with the group, perhaps being slightly more willing to consider Absalon data given that we already have some insight into student engagement through advising appointments. But yes - an opt-out is crucial for all this.

Thanks everyone. I agree with A2 about Q3 being really challenging – especially given my own experience dropping out and restarting a program. “Improvement” felt loaded; it’s easy to get caught up in numbers when actually what matters is helping *individuals*.

I think Q4, explainability, is incredibly important for me too. Being flagged feels vulnerable, so understanding *why* would be vital for trusting any support offered. I was more cautious than most on the data additions – my answers reflected that. 

Seeing almost everyone reject age, gender and race validated my discomfort. And the idea of an opt-out is essential; it gives students agency over their own data and builds trust. It's a good way to address some of those inherent power imbalances.

Defining ‘improvement’ isn't about statistics; it's about genuinely supporting students who are struggling, and that requires nuance. Seeing the strong rejection of sensitive data is reassuring, although my slightly more open stance on first-generation status and financial aid reflects a recognition those students often face systemic barriers.
